<reason>A built the debate's most elegant structure — the fork that earlier disclosure is either harmful (menu-level, contingent fees) or useless (cart-level, anchor already set) — and pressed it with sharp symmetry arguments. But B dismantled both horns more convincingly than A defended them. Against the "useless" horn, B showed anchoring recalibrates with each new number, so earlier accurate figures inform more decisions while less is sunk, and turned A's own logic: payment-stage disclosure is the worst point on the spectrum, so earlier is a strict improvement. Against the "harmful" horn, B's conditional menu policy ("18% for parties of 6+") was a genuinely third option — accurate, itemized, cheap — that dissolved the worst-case-estimate/folded-price dilemma; A's retort that this is a "fee schedule, not a charge" leaned on a strained reading of the motion and sat in tension with A's own claim that bistros already print such policies (if so, the burden vanishes too). B also neutralized the small-business burden (UI change for apps, one menu line for restaurants), which A partly conceded in A2.5. A's closing overstated the record — claiming B conceded the motion was "impossible" and that costs were "never answered" — when B had answered both directly. B's closing reframe (the baseline is the status quo, not perfection) crystallized the decisive comparison. Both sides clipped one turn and both executed Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 formats cleanly; the execution costs roughly wash.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 answer on the restaurant case (B4.3–B4.5): the conditional, itemized menu disclosure as a third option collapsed the "harmful" horn of A's fork — the load-bearing structure of A's entire case — and A's "fee schedule isn't a charge" response never recovered the contingency argument it had originally staked.</best_rebuttal>
